definition: Oscillate means to swing back and forth between two positions or states.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word oscillate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know oscillate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The desk lamp hung from the tent pole and oscillated with every gust, swinging its shadow from one wall to the other.
Quiver is milder than oscillate — a quivering needle trembles around one spot, while an oscillating one sweeps the whole dial between its two ends.
Careen is stronger than oscillate — an oscillating swing is regular and bounded, but something careening slings itself about with no rhythm and no fixed stops.

Swing is the plain word for moving to and fro — a gate can swing once and stop, and nothing fixes where it goes. Oscillate is stricter: it requires two set poles and a repeated return trip between them, often on a rhythm steady enough to time.

To shuttle is to travel back and forth between two places, like a ferry or an airport bus, and the word stays physical — bodies and vehicles shuttle. Oscillate covers the same two-pole round trip but reaches further: needles, voltages, moods, and undecided minds all oscillate.
to come to rest at one position and stay
to keep moving steadily in a single direction

The swinging little oscillum stayed a one-word family: outside oscillate and its own offspring, oscillation and oscillator, the root built nothing else in English. Meet oscill- and you are always looking at the same swinging mask.
Oscillate means to swing back and forth between two positions or states.
The broken thermostat made the office oscillate between sauna and icebox — twenty minutes of roasting, a clank from the vents, twenty of shivering, and back, all winter long.
Oscillate needs exactly two poles: back and forth, A to B and home again, often on a rhythm you could set a watch by.
Movement that wanders with no fixed endpoints is mere fluctuation; the pendulum, the metronome, and the undecided mind all oscillate because they keep returning to the same two stations.
Oscillate is precise: two poles and a return trip, often on a rhythm.
Engineers give it to circuits and pendulums; writers borrow it for moods and negotiations that keep swinging between the same two states.
For an undecided person specifically, vacillate — a word you met earlier in this course — stresses the indecision; oscillate stresses the motion.

By mid-morning, with commuters crossing in step, the deck began to oscillate: it leaned a hand's width toward the east rail, then the west, then east again, on a beat you could count.
A junior engineer timed it.
The trip from one extreme to the other took just under two seconds, and the deck repeated the trip without variation.
'It isn't drifting and it isn't shaking at random,' she wrote in the log.
'It travels between the same two limits, over and over.' Dampers went in that week, and the deck's steady two-ended motion faded to an occasional shiver.
